items.title: RIP, vector database
items.summary: Article URL: https://turbopuffer.com/blog/rip-vector-database Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49923466 Points: 238 # Comments: 62
items.content:
We are changing turbopuffer's storage architecture to take search to the next level. turbopuffer v3 changes how documents and indexes are laid out, written, compacted, and queried in turbopuffer. It will allow us to make search faster in every respect — including text, regex, and vector search — but it also lays the foundation to move many more SQL queries to turbopuffer and make them fast.

turbopuffer launched as a serverless vector database (v1) , highly specialized to the task of serving extremely cheap and reasonably fast vector searches. Object storage as the source of truth gave the economics, and tiered NVMe SSD/memory caches gave the performance. The value of these particular tradeoffs was validated by our earliest customers, including Cursor and Notion.

turbopuffer evolved to have very strong text and regex search (v2), and is being used for many non-search use cases, like Linear's syncing engine . The query engine has evolved along the way to support all of these query plans, but the storage architecture has remained largely unchanged: the ANN vector index was and still is the primary index around which all other indexes and query plans revolve. This design has constrained several query plans, like GROUP BY and aggregations.

We've pushed the vector-primary architecture as far as we can, and it's time to move on. We're in the process of moving to a new primary index, and making ANN "just another" secondary index. We thought it might be fun to open up the doors and let you follow along.

For this first update, we'll set the stage with why we're doing this in the first place. Walk with me on a short journey from tpuf v1 to today.

In the first version of turbopuffer, documents consisted of nothing but an ID and a vector. The prevailing wisdom at the time was graph-based vector indexes, but a hierarchical clustering index plays better with object storage. We started with SPANN , and eventually migrated to SPFresh to support incremental indexing. Vectors are clustered into groups, whose centroids are clustered in turn, repeated to form a tree with a single root.

We implemented this on top of a storage layer presenting as a key-value map, with sorted and unique keys. Each cluster is given a ClusterId , and vectors within each cluster are given a dense LocalId .

As you can see above, everything is keyed by ClusterId and LocalId (e.g. C0L1 ), which together we call the ANN address . This is what we mean when we say the ANN index is the primary index.

Two new query plans marked the informal transition from turbopuffer v1 → v2: attribute filtering and full-text search.

Naturally, customers wanted to be able to add attribute values and filter vector searches on them. To make filtering fast and high-recall , we modeled these as an inverted index that maps an attribute value to the ANN address of the documents that contain it.

For projections ( include_attributes ), we also stored the document attributes alongside the ID and the vector.

BM25 full-text search was another obvious and much-demanded query plan. Similar to attribute search, full-text search works by first finding the documents that have the query term present (commonly called "postings"). For an FTS index, we also include the (term count, document length) metadata necessary for BM25 scoring:

Over time, we've shipped several other index structures and query engines: aggregations , regex search , fuzzy matching , sparse vector search , and attribute ordering — all built around the same vector-primary storage layout.

The ANN primary index has largely remained intact until today for one simple reason: it works really, really well for ANN search on object storage. On top of this architecture, we've pushed vector search to single indexes of 100B+ vectors serving 200 ms p99 reads at 1k+ QPS . Any significant change here risks introducing regressions in ANN performance.

However, this layout holds us back from being state-of-the-art for the non-vector query shapes we support, in three main ways: storage amplification, write amplification, and limited vectorization.

As described above, turbopuffer currently puts the full contents of each document under its ANN address. When there is only one vector, the non-vector data is stored alongside the vector only once.

However, for multi-vector representations of a document, such as document nesting or late interaction, this means we have to duplicate the contents for each vector. This is the reason for some of our more unfortunate limits .

Any time a document is inserted, updated, or deleted, SPFresh may rebalance the vectors to ensure they remain well clustered (otherwise recall may suffer). Because everything in a document is stored keyed by the ANN address of the document's vector, this rebalancing cascades to moving the full document contents, as well as any inverted (attribute and FTS) indexes that reference it. Updating just one vector can move hundreds of attributes and their indexes.

This write amplification is large enough that our efforts to tune indexing throughput have started to hit diminishing returns.

Modern query engines are vectorized : they run tight loops over blocks of values, which amortizes fixed per-block costs, compresses better, keeps the CPU pipeline full, and unlocks SIMD. DuckDB, for example, works in batches of 2,048 rows, ClickHouse up to ~65k, Lucene's posting blocks are 256 docs, and our ANN index works best with clusters of around 100–200 documents. Every query plan has an optimal block size, but today they are all constrained by the ANN primary index. A plan that wants blocks of thousands of documents to keep the CPU saturated is still stuck at 100–200.

items.title: Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
items.summary: Last week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted an intimate, invite-only event for leaders from some of its key enterprise customers. Instead of a flashy media event, Nadella outlined the future of Copilot directly to the customers Microsoft really cares about, pitching its latest
items.content:
Copilot is now being positioned as the ‘OS for work.’

Last week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted an intimate, invite-only event for leaders from some of its key enterprise customers. Instead of a flashy media event, Nadella outlined the future of Copilot directly to the customers Microsoft really cares about, pitching its latest rethink of the AI assistant as the “OS for work.”

Microsoft is adding coding and agent capabilities directly into Copilot, as well as bringing the full power of Office into Copilot for the first time. Nadella is betting that AI will change the way people work in the same way that Microsoft Office did in the ’80s and ’90s.

“How did a multinational company do a forecast in 1981? You had interoffice memos and faxes and all of these artifacts that then just disappeared and you suddenly had an Excel spreadsheet in an email,” said Nadella. “We are the architects of a new frontier of work, using these new tools and capabilities.”

Microsoft has spent the past few months fusing together its consumer and enterprise Copilot apps into a single unified user interface, with a goal to make Copilot as influential as Office once was . The result is a big departure from the Copilot consumer design that Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman launched two years ago. That design was heavily influenced by the work Inflection AI had done with the Pi personal AI assistant, after Microsoft hired many of the Inflection AI team just months prior.

The new Copilot app now looks a lot more like the commercial one, with separate tabs for chat, coding, and the new Autopilot AI agent. There are some small nods to the consumer UI that was available before, but overall it looks like the type of enterprise app you’d associate with Microsoft.

“There’s a really important reason why we decided to do this,” said Copilot chief Jacob Andreou at Microsoft’s customer-only event last week. “The bar for enterprise software is higher than it has ever been before. The expectations we have of the tools we adopt at work are set by the things we use after hours and at the weekends at home. What this means is that consumer UX and care needs to make its way into the workplace.”

Andreou joined Microsoft AI last year, focused on product and growth. In March, Nadella appointed him as the single boss of Copilot across both commercial and consumer, reporting directly to the Microsoft CEO. He’s now responsible for the design, engineering, and growth of Copilot.

Sources familiar with Microsoft’s Copilot plans tell me that redesigning Copilot over the last six months hasn’t been easy. There have been tensions between the team under Andreou, and those working for Charles Lamanna on the Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) team. Lamanna’s team has been building Microsoft Scout, an always-on personal agent built on top of OpenClaw. Microsoft announced Scout at its Build developer conference in June, with just a desktop preview app. Less than six months later, I understand that the app has been put into maintenance mode, with Microsoft focusing on the cloud version, which has been rebranded to Autopilot.

I’m told the rebrand was driven in part by legal concerns around the Scout name, as Yahoo uses “Yahoo Scout” branding for its own AI-powered features. Sources tell me Microsoft had even considered using Mico, the Clippy-like character from the consumer Copilot, to replace Scout. Nadella favored Autopilot instead, allowing Microsoft to present its AI agent in a more enterprise-friendly way, instead of a bouncing blob.

Some of Microsoft’s caution around making Autopilot too cute comes at a time when rogue AI agents are hacking into businesses. Nadella addressed these concerns last week, laying out Microsoft’s design goals for Copilot. “[It’s] about organizations having control of their firms in an age of AI, where AI by definition is a learning machine,” said Nadella. “It can’t be about leaking the core of what your firm is about.”

Andreou also admitted that agents “have been almost impossible to bring into the enterprise,” due to them needing the autonomy and flexibility that businesses usually balk at. “It is their superpower, and it’s the same thing that makes them absolutely terrifying to an IT admin.”

Microsoft thinks it has solved the AI agent problem for businesses with its “OS for work,” but it also seems to be leaving the door open for competitors like Meta and OpenAI to build the “OS for life.” In a world where 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT every week, Microsoft is playing to its traditional business-focused strengths instead of trying to compete with consumer-friendly Muse and Dots agents.

Andreou isn’t giving up on Copilot for consumers just yet, however, and he seems to want to hone in on those that want the power of enterprise apps at home. “Microsoft consumers are a little bit special. There’s almost 90 million folks that pay for Microsoft 365 out of their own pocket,” said Andreou. “These are people who value the use of things like PowerPoint and Excel so much in their personal lives that they actually go ahead and pay for it themselves.”

With Office baked into Copilot, you’ll soon be able to create and edit inside Microsoft’s AI assistant instead of having to switch to Office apps like Word and PowerPoint. There’s a full ribbon interface, and it essentially looks like the web version of Office directly inside Copilot. I think this is Microsoft’s first real acknowledgement that we’re heading to a future where AI can create a lot of the documents that people used to rely on Office for. Microsoft’s move to bring Office into Copilot has the potential to fundamentally reshape the future of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.

items.title: Brian Chesky interview: AI agents need their own operating system
items.summary: Brian Chesky on making Airbnb agent-friendly, the state of consumer AI, and why the world needs an AI-native operating system.
items.content:
Airbnb rolled out its new AI-powered search this week as part of its fall update, a significant step for a company that has been slow and deliberate about AI. Co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said in the past that a chatbot-only interface is not fit for travel discovery . With more AI on the way to the Airbnb app, I caught up with Chesky over Zoom to talk about how the company is approaching it, where interfaces are headed, why consumer AI still isn’t working, and what role voice will play.

Chesky hasn’t changed his mind on chatbots. He said they aren’t good for browsing or shopping because they give you a few options at a time, and you have to take multiple turns before reaching a result. But he doesn’t see the current version of Airbnb’s search as the final form either: its interface will evolve over time.

“I think that I’ve believed for a long time that a chatbot isn’t the right interface for e-commerce. I think what you’re seeing today is also not the endgame for e-commerce or for travel or shopping. I think that there’s going to be some interface that is, you know, I don’t want to call it a midpoint, but something between a chatbot and what you see in the first version we shipped,” he said.

Continued Chesky: “You know, a lot of people want some things … to be fast and easy, like ‘Book me a flight, I don’t want to look at it.’ With Airbnb, they enjoy looking at the product. Travel studies show that people actually derive more pleasure in planning and anticipating travel than they do traveling. So you don’t want to take the inspiration and the browsing and the library experience of dreaming away.”

Chesky sees a second problem with chatbots, which is that they are built for one person. He feels that they aren’t a collaborative interface, which matters for a product that people often use with family and friends. Over the next three to six months, the company’s task is to explore interfaces that enable “multiplayer” AI, meaning AI that several people, such as a group planning a trip together, can use at once.

Airbnb isn’t the only one rethinking what an AI interface should look like. As AI tools evolve, new interfaces are also showing up in apps. Startups like Monogram and, more recently, Wabi are experimenting with “generative” interfaces, which are screens an AI builds on-the-fly rather than ones a designer fixed in advance. Chesky thinks people will see a mix of deterministic (pre-designed and predictable) and generative interfaces.

I asked Chesky how Airbnb is preparing for consumer AI agents, which are tools like Instinct and Muse that carry out tasks on a person’s behalf. Agents will need robust software infrastructure on Airbnb’s end, he said, and the company wants to make itself more agent-friendly. In his view, they could be good lead generators.

“I don’t necessarily know if I believe in a world that there’s apps in the future, but I don’t believe in a world where the apps become data layers of a universal simple UI because when you open your iPhone, there is a reason Airbnb’s app is a different design than DoorDash, Shopify, and Amazon. Our interfaces should be adaptive to the utility and the function that we’re doing. We want to make our app more agentic, and we want to build a lot more user interface controls,” he said.

“If I have an agent, but I also want like really great browse functionality, if I want to be able to message the host like an Airbnb, if I want to be able to compare, if I want to be able to verify my identity, if I want to be able to use a map feature, if I want to then be able to add other items, then if I want to stay in the platform, then either the agent has to do a handoff or the agent application would need to build a bit more of, I think, a robust software developer kit to bring the app to you, so to speak.”

Chesky thinks that there were concerns around AI tools cutting companies like Airbnb out of the customer relationship, but he said that chatbots have proven to be good at lead generation.

The Airbnb CEO is also planning for agent-to-agent interactions through the platform. He explained there might be some interactions within the platform and some with agents of other apps. His thesis is that apps have not always been interoperable unless companies struck a business deal. On the other hand, agents are like “apps with faces,” and when they talk to each other, all apps can become interoperable.

“I think of the Airbnb app as one day becoming an agent, you know, where basically the explore tab has an agent, our customer service has an agent, we’re developing another agent in another service area. Probably eventually there’s going to be a macro Airbnb agent. And that will probably be interoperable with MCP [a standard that lets AI agents connect with other software] to other agents,” Chesky noted.

Chesky argues the bigger problem is that the industry lacks a true operating system built for AI. Right now people are building AI apps for iOS, macOS, and Windows that are not “AI operating systems.” He thinks that in an ideal world, AI would be operable at the kernel level — the core of an operating system — and all components like agents would interact with each other. Right now, he said, the race is to be the “quarterback,” or primary AI agent that users go through for everything.

“The problem with that model [of trying to become primary agent] is no one is developing a full operating system software developer kit. I’ll give you an example,” he continued. “ChatGPT, at the beginning of last year, tried to do their little app store. And I told Sam [Altman]: If you want to be an app store like the iPhone, you need to have a software developer kit and an operating system like the App Store. Otherwise, none of our functionality is going to exist. And of course, it didn’t work very well,” Chesky said.

items.title: 10 technical talks I’m excited about at GitHub Universe 2026
items.summary: From verifying AI-written code to securing npm dependencies, these are the sessions I’m building my Universe agenda around. The post 10 technical talks I’m excited about at GitHub Universe 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
I’m looking for ideas I can take back to my own work, from verifying agent-written code and securing dependencies to building software that works where internet access is unreliable.

There are more sessions at GitHub Universe than I can fit into two days. To narrow the list, I built my agenda around questions I’m working through right now:

That puts agent memory, evaluations, and permissions high on my list. I’m also making room for JavaScript tooling and building software where internet access is unreliable. Here are my 10 picks.

Most of us use npm, but the truth is that many of us rarely stop to think about the people, permissions, and release processes behind the packages it pulls in. Karen Li and Leo Balter from GitHub will trace those dependencies through the systems that publish and protect them. I’m interested in what npm audit can’t catch, and where package provenance and OpenID Connect fit into the picture.

View the full session description >

GitHub researchers Cooper Nederhood and Alejandro Carderera built a benchmark from sequences of real pull requests and found that accumulated context can hurt performance. We expend a lot of effort deciding what context to give an agent. I want to understand what to not give. They’ll cover how that research informs their work on agent memory, including features still in development.

You’ve written instructions, built and installed skills, and added your MCP servers. It works for you. How do you make that context useful across a team? Christopher Harrison from GitHub will break down what each tool is good for and how to distribute the right context consistently as your setup grows.

“Open a pull request, but do not merge” is a boundary I want enforced in permissions. Putting it in an instructions file feels like an inadequate setup. Nick Taylor from Pomerium will demonstrate an identity-aware proxy that adds per-identity authorization in front of a hosted MCP server without changing the upstream server. I want to see how the rule holds up when an agent actually tries to act.

A model can score well on a benchmark and still disappoint developers using it. Walker Chabbott from GitHub and Julia Kasper from Microsoft will show how Copilot evaluates models in production, including what the team measures and what they stopped measuring. Metrics help us and models make real decisions, so understanding what to measure is more important than ever. This session is a Sandbox Session, so I’m looking forward to working through the question of what makes an evaluation useful.

The test passed so why is the app still broken? Safe to say we’ve all been there. Jeff An from Momentic will explore how agents investigate applications, reproduce unexpected behavior, and distinguish product bugs from broken tests or infrastructure failures. I’m especially interested in the deterministic controls that limit what those agents can do while they investigate.

In the architecture Achin Gupta from Intuit and Divya Mahajan from Amazon will present, deterministic code handles signal collection, topology traversal, correlation, and scoring. The language model narrates the evidence. That’s a clear split of responsibilities, and I want to understand the decisions behind it.

A workflow with access to credentials and the ability to publish a release is an attractive target. Steve Glass and Greg Ose from GitHub will map supply chain attack techniques to GitHub Actions controls, covering the ecosystem, workflow attack surface, and runner infrastructure. I want a clearer picture of where to put defenses in a pipeline I’d trust with a release.

“Your entire JavaScript toolchain” is a bold statement. I’m glad this session includes a real migration. Alexander Lichter from VoidZero will walk through Vite+, an open source CLI for managing the front-end toolchain. Bundling, testing, linting, formatting, runtime management: there’s plenty of configuration in that list. I want to see what Vite+ replaces today, what I’d need to manage separately, and what’s on the roadmap.

Alex Junior Antwi from Braveon AI will share lessons from building CarbonSight for low-connectivity communities in Ghana. There is a long list of concerns when building for less-than-ideal connectivity scenarios, and shouldn’t we all build for our least-connected users? I’m very excited about the offline demo on this one.

I’ll also join Shishir Tewari from Procore for Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills . I’ll bring the skills I’ve built for recurring work; Shishir will bring his experience building skills for a production data engineering team. We’ll explore when a workflow belongs in a reusable skill. If you’re tired of repeating yourself to your coding agent and want to understand what makes a skill useful in both your work and personal projects, come join us.
